title: Bread with no time to rise (Exodus 12:33–42)
hookLine: dough on their shoulders, and a mixed multitude going with them

cards: The taxi's downstairs. The flight is in two hours. Somebody is grabbing half-packed bags, leaving dishes in the sink, the bread they meant to bake still sitting in a bowl.
After generations in Egypt, it happens to a whole people in one night. Pharaoh, broken, calls Moses and Aaron in the night: get out, all of you, go. The Egyptians push them to hurry.
And the dough for tomorrow's bread hasn't risen yet.

teach.b: The Torah paints it in one detail: "And the people took their dough before it was leavened," their kneading bowls wrapped in their cloaks, on their shoulders.
When they stop to eat, they bake the dough into flat cakes, because they "could not tarry." That's matzah: flour and water, baked before it can rise.
Every year at Passover, Jews eat it, and many clear leavened bread from their homes for the whole week. Here's the interesting part: matzah means two opposite things at once.
Early in the seder, people lift it up and call it the bread of affliction, a phrase from Deuteronomy: the poor bread of slaves.

Later the same evening, the Haggadah explains it another way: the bread of freedom, dough that had no time to rise before they were set free. Same bread. It depends on which side of the door you're on.

Then a small detail that's easy to miss: "And a mixed multitude went up also with them." Not only the children of Israel. Maybe Egyptians, maybe other slaves, people who had seen what happened and decided to go.
The Torah doesn't explain who, and it doesn't turn them away.
And the text counts the time: four hundred and thirty years, and on that very day, they went out. It calls that night a night of watching, kept by God, and kept by the people ever after.
When the moment came, they didn't wait for the bread to be perfect. They went.

how: During the week of Passover Jews eat matzah and remove leavened bread, chametz, from their homes; at the seder the matzah is lifted and called the bread of affliction.

practice: Think of something you've been holding back until it's perfect: a message you keep rewriting, a plan you keep refining, a step you're waiting to feel ready for. Ask yourself whether it's ready enough; flat bread still feeds people.
Decide on one thing you'll let go of as it is.
